Since the standard basis spans $\mathbb R^d$, this finite Gram–Schmidt procedure produces an orthonormal basis whose first vector is $u$. Let $Q$ be the associated orthogonal coordinate map. If $d=1$, take $Qx=ux$. In either case the first coordinate of $Qx$ is $u\cdot x$, and [F4] says $Q$ preserves Lebesgue measure.

Fix an integer $R\ge1$. Since $Q$ is a finite matrix, choose $C_R<\infty$ greater than $R$ times the largest sum of absolute entries in any row; then $Q([-R,R]^d)\subseteq[-C_R,C_R]^d$. Since $E$ has outer measure zero, [F1] makes it Lebesgue measurable and null. Thus $E_R=((E-b)/\lVert w\rVert_2)\cap[-C_R,C_R]$ is a one-dimensional measurable null set by [F5]. By [F1], choose a Borel null set $B_R\supseteq E_R$. If $d=1$, the image under $Q$ of the set in the Statement intersected with $[-R,R]$ is contained in $B_R$. If $d\ge2$, that image is contained in $B_R\times[-C_R,C_R]^{d-1}$.

If $d=1$, the bounded pullback image is contained in the Borel null set $B_R$, and the inverse orthogonal map preserves nullity by [F4]. If $d\ge2$, the Borel set $B_R\times[-C_R,C_R]^{d-1}$ is Lebesgue measurable by [F7]; both Lebesgue factors are $\sigma$-finite by [F8], so Tonelli [F2] gives it product measure zero because its one-dimensional section factor $B_R$ has measure zero, and [F3] identifies that product measure with $\lambda_d$. The full pullback is the countable union of its intersections with $[-R,R]^d$, $R\ge1$. Each intersection is a subset of the Borel null set from step 3.1, hence is measurable and null by [F6]. The full pullback is measurable by [F6] and null by countable subadditivity [F9]. If two functions differ only on $E$, their compositions differ only on this pullback, proving the consequence.

$$p_m(\varphi)=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_{x\in K}|\partial^\alpha\varphi(x)|,\qquad d(\varphi,\psi)=\sum_{m=0}^\infty2^{-m-1}\min(1,p_m(\varphi-\psi)).$$

The topology is generated by the seminorms $p_m$: neighborhoods at zero contain finite intersections of $p_m<\varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon>0$. Derivatives are continuous on $K$, so these suprema are finite; for $K=\varnothing$ all suprema are defined as zero and $\mathcal D_K=\{0\}$. For nonempty $K$, $p_0$ separates functions because all functions vanish off $K$. These are increasing seminorms and the displayed series converges since its terms are at most $2^{-m-1}$.

The term **fixed-support Fréchet space** refers to this topology and metric. Their agreement and completeness are established by the registered justifier [[lem-fixed-support-test-function-spaces-are-complete]], rather than included as unproved consequences of the name. If $K$ has empty interior, every test supported in $K$ is zero: a nonzero continuous value would have a neighborhood of nonzero values inside $K$.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field (Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)) and let
$\varepsilon \in F$ with $\varepsilon > 0$. Then there is a natural number
$n \ge 1$ such that

$$\frac{1}{n \cdot 1_F} < \varepsilon ,$$

where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of $F$ (Every complete ordered field is Archimedean) and
$1/(n \cdot 1_F)$ is its multiplicative inverse (Field). As is standard
we abbreviate $n \cdot 1_F$ to $n$ and write the conclusion $1/n < \varepsilon$.

This is the **reciprocal form** of the Archimedean property.
Every complete ordered field is Archimedean on its own delivers only the assertion that the canonical
naturals are cofinal, $x < n \cdot 1_F$; the form actually used in analysis, that
the reciprocals of the naturals get below every positive bound, is the statement
above, and it is recorded separately so that no proof has to reconstruct the
inversion step in passing.

Put $e=\varphi-q_0$. Then $e^{(M)}=\varphi^{(M)}-p$ and $e^{(j)}(a)=0$ for $j<M$. For a distribution $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ in the convention of [[def-distribution]] and a multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, its **distributional derivative** is
$$\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)).$$
The test derivative is a continuous linear endomorphism by [[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]. Its composition with $u$, multiplied by the indicated sign, is therefore a continuous complex-linear functional, so this definition produces a distribution. The pairing is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. For $\alpha=0$ the operation is the identity; for one coordinate derivative its sign is minus. Distributional derivatives satisfy $\partial^\alpha\partial^\beta u=\partial^{\alpha+\beta}u$ and are continuous linear maps on $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ for both the weak and strong distribution topologies. Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $f=\sum_{i\ge0}a_i x^i\in R[x]$. Its **formal derivative** is

$$ f':=\sum_{i\ge1} i a_i x^{i-1}. $$

Here $i a_i$ means the sum of $i$ copies of $a_i$ in the additive group of $R$. Equivalently, the coefficient of $x^n$ in $f'$ is $(n+1)a_{n+1}$. Partition $[-M,M]$ into finitely many intervals of length at most $\delta$ and replace each value of $f_M$ by a fixed endpoint of its interval. If $\mu(K)>0$, choose $\delta$ with $\delta\mu(K)^{1/p}<\varepsilon/2$; if $\mu(K)=0$, any $\delta>0$ suffices. Since $\mu$ is concentrated on $K$, replace $s$ by $\mathbf1_Ks$: this finite Borel simple function represents the same class and admits a representation with every set $E_j\subseteq K$. Write such a simple function as $s=\sum_{j=1}^N c_j\mathbf 1_{E_j}$ with Borel $E_j\subseteq K$. Assume Countable Choice for the Lebesgue-measure convention. A real-valued function $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ belongs to the activation class $\mathcal M$ when it is Lebesgue measurable, is locally essentially bounded, and the closure of its discontinuity set has one-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero. Here locally essentially bounded means that for every compact interval $J\subset\mathbb R$ there is a finite $M_J$ such that $|\sigma(t)|\le M_J$ for Lebesgue-almost every $t\in J$. The discontinuity set is $\{t:\sigma\text{ is not continuous at }t\}$. The function is a polynomial almost everywhere when there is a real algebraic polynomial $p$ such that $\sigma=p$ outside a Lebesgue-null set.

The subclass $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{pt}}$ consists of those $\sigma\in\mathcal M$ that are also pointwise locally bounded: $\sup_{t\in J}|\sigma(t)|<\infty$ for every compact interval $J$. This extra condition distinguishes pointwise uniform approximation from approximation in the essential-supremum norm.

For open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, write $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ when $f:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is Lebesgue measurable and $\int_K|f|<\infty$ for every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$. This extends [[def-locally-integrable-function-on-r-n]]: equivalently, require integrability on every ball whose closure is a compact subset of $\Omega$. Such balls finitely cover each compact $K$, and conversely their closures are compact; on all of $\mathbb R^n$, any ball lies in a larger compact closed ball.

For a test $\varphi$ as in [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]], define the **regular functional**

$$\langle u_f,\varphi\rangle=\int_\Omega f(x)\varphi(x)\,dx.$$

This is well-defined since $|\int f\varphi|\le\sup_K|\varphi|\int_K|f|$ for $K=\operatorname{supp}\varphi$. It is complex-linear in $f$ and in $\varphi$ and depends only on the almost-everywhere class of $f$. For an empty support the integral is zero. The subsequent embedding theorem establishes continuity, so that this is a distribution, and injectivity modulo almost-everywhere equality. That theorem states the Countable Choice cost of its injectivity proof; no choice is needed to define the displayed pairing.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. The map $f\mapsto u_f$, $u_f(\varphi)=\int_\Omega f\varphi$, is a complex-linear injection from $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ modulo almost-everywhere equality into $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$. It is continuous from the local $L^1$ topology, generated by $f\mapsto\int_K|f|$ for compact $K\subseteq\Omega$, to the strong distribution topology. In particular local $L^1$ convergence implies strong distribution convergence. The continuity estimate itself is choice-free; Countable Choice is used in the cited $L^1$ approximate-identity theorem proving injectivity.

For an integer $n\ge1$, a compact $K\subseteq\Omega$, and an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, put $\mathcal D_K=\{\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega):\operatorname{supp}\varphi\subseteq K\}$, using [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]. For integers $m\ge0$ set

$$p_m(\varphi)=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_{x\in K}|\partial^\alpha\varphi(x)|,\qquad d(\varphi,\psi)=\sum_{m=0}^\infty2^{-m-1}\min(1,p_m(\varphi-\psi)).$$

The topology is generated by the seminorms $p_m$: neighborhoods at zero contain finite intersections of $p_m<\varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon>0$. Derivatives are continuous on $K$, so these suprema are finite; for $K=\varnothing$ all suprema are defined as zero and $\mathcal D_K=\{0\}$. For nonempty $K$, $p_0$ separates functions because all functions vanish off $K$. These are increasing seminorms and the displayed series converges since its terms are at most $2^{-m-1}$.

The term **fixed-support Fréchet space** refers to this topology and metric. Their agreement and completeness are established by the registered justifier [[lem-fixed-support-test-function-spaces-are-complete]], rather than included as unproved consequences of the name. If $K$ has empty interior, every test supported in $K$ is zero: a nonzero continuous value would have a neighborhood of nonzero values inside $K$.

For every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$ with $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ open, the space $\mathcal D_K$ is Hausdorff, locally convex and complete for

is integrable there, and its Lebesgue integral equals its Riemann integral:
$$\int_{[a,b]} f\,d\lambda_1=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.$$

This is the point at which the completeness of Lebesgue measure is used
essentially: the proof obtains a Borel function equal to $f$ almost everywhere,
and measurability of $f$ itself is then a completeness statement.

measurable or not,

$$\lambda_n^*(E) \;=\; \inf\,\{\, \lambda_n(U) \;:\; U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n \text{ open and } E \subseteq U \,\},$$

the infimum being taken in $[0,+\infty]$ over a family that is nonempty because

derivations.claim: Let $T_\sigma$ be the regular distribution induced by $\sigma$. It is real by [F9]. The hypothesis of the Statement includes all real-valued test functions. Applying [F2] to that subclass gives $N\in\mathbb N_0$ such that every real-test convolution supported in $[-1,1]$ is a polynomial of degree at most $N$. By [F7], choose a nonnegative smooth bump supported in $(-1,1)$ and divide by its positive finite integral to obtain the real unit-mass test $\rho$. Its rescalings $\rho_\varepsilon$ for $0<\varepsilon\le1$ remain supported in $[-1,1]$, so $g_\varepsilon=\sigma*\rho_\varepsilon$ is a polynomial of degree at most $N$.

By [F3], the regular distributions induced by $g_\varepsilon$ converge to $T_\sigma$ on every test function. For every $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$, the definition [F8] and this convergence give $\langle D^{N+1}T_\sigma,\psi\rangle=(-1)^{N+1}\langle T_\sigma,\psi^{(N+1)}\rangle=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}(-1)^{N+1}\int g_\varepsilon(x)\psi^{(N+1)}(x)\,dx=0$, because [F6] makes each integral zero for the polynomial $g_\varepsilon$ of degree at most $N$. Thus $D^{N+1}T_\sigma=0$.

By [F4], $T_\sigma$ is the regular distribution of a polynomial $p$. Since both $\sigma$ and $p$ are locally integrable, injectivity [F5] implies $\sigma=p$ almost everywhere. This proves the forward implication; its contrapositive is the equivalent existence assertion.

Let $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ and $\varphi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^n)$. On the open safe domain $V=\{x:x-\operatorname{supp}\varphi\subseteq\Omega\}$, the convolution $u*\varphi$ is smooth and
$$\partial^\alpha(u*\varphi)=(\partial^\alpha u)*\varphi=u*(\partial^\alpha\varphi).$$
The last expression is restricted to $V$ if its own safe domain is larger. For $\Omega=\mathbb R^n$ the domain is all of $\mathbb R^n$. This holds in ZF.

Let $g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be infinitely differentiable and not a polynomial. For every $d\ge1$ and compact $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, scalar networks with one hidden layer, activation $g$, arbitrary affine hidden inputs and linear output are uniformly dense in $C(K,\mathbb R)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\sigma\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{pt}}$, let $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$, and let $K\subseteq\mathbb R$ be compact. Define the convolution

$$g(x)=\int_{\mathbb R}\sigma(x-t)\varphi(t)\,dt.$$

Then $\operatorname{Re}g$ and $\operatorname{Im}g$ are each uniform limits on $K$ of finite sums $x\mapsto c+\sum_{j=1}^m a_j\sigma(x+b_j)$ with real coefficients, hence of single-hidden-layer networks with activation $\sigma$. In particular, if $\varphi$ is real-valued, then $g$ itself is such a uniform limit.

Assume Countable Choice for the Lebesgue-measure convention. A real-valued function $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ belongs to the activation class $\mathcal M$ when it is Lebesgue measurable, is locally essentially bounded, and the closure of its discontinuity set has one-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero. Here locally essentially bounded means that for every compact interval $J\subset\mathbb R$ there is a finite $M_J$ such that $|\sigma(t)|\le M_J$ for Lebesgue-almost every $t\in J$. The discontinuity set is $\{t:\sigma\text{ is not continuous at }t\}$. The function is a polynomial almost everywhere when there is a real algebraic polynomial $p$ such that $\sigma=p$ outside a Lebesgue-null set.

The subclass $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{pt}}$ consists of those $\sigma\in\mathcal M$ that are also pointwise locally bounded: $\sup_{t\in J}|\sigma(t)|<\infty$ for every compact interval $J$. This extra condition distinguishes pointwise uniform approximation from approximation in the essential-supremum norm.

derivations.claim: By [F2] and the hypothesis on $\sigma$, some real test function $\varphi_*$ supported in $[-1,1]$ has a nonpolynomial convolution $g_*=\sigma*\varphi_*$. Indeed, if every real test had polynomial convolution, then for every complex test $\varphi=\varphi_R+i\varphi_I$ both real convolutions would be polynomials, making every complex convolution polynomial; [F2] would then imply that $\sigma$ is polynomial almost everywhere. By [F3], $g_*$ is smooth. The activation hypothesis has the content in [F6].

By [F4], choose a finite $g_*$-network $G(x)=c+\sum_{j=1}^m a_jg_*(w_j\cdot x+b_j)$ with $\sup_{x\in K}|G(x)-f(x)|<\varepsilon/2$. For each $j$ with $a_j\ne0$ and $w_j\ne0$, the set $w_j\cdot K+b_j$ is compact and lies in a compact interval $I_j$.

By [F5], for each such $j$ choose a finite sum of translates of $\sigma$ uniformly within $\varepsilon/(2(1+\sum_{j=1}^m|a_j|))$ of $g_*$ on $I_j$. Composing with $w_j\cdot x+b_j$ gives a finite sum of units $\sigma(w_j\cdot x+b_j-t)$; units with $w_j=0$ contribute only constants and are absorbed into the output bias. Summing the finitely many approximants yields a $\sigma$-network $N$ with $\sup_K|N-G|<\varepsilon/2$.
The triangle inequality gives $\sup_K|N-f|\le\sup_K|N-G|+\sup_K|G-f|<\varepsilon$. Hence the $\sigma$-network family is uniformly dense on $K$.

citations.quote:
Assume Countable Choice for the Lebesgue-measure convention. A real-valued function $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ belongs to the activation class $\mathcal M$ when it is Lebesgue measurable, is locally essentially bounded, and the closure of its discontinuity set has one-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero. Here locally essentially bounded means that for every compact interval $J\subset\mathbb R$ there is a finite $M_J$ such that $|\sigma(t)|\le M_J$ for Lebesgue-almost every $t\in J$. The discontinuity set is $\{t:\sigma\text{ is not continuous at }t\}$. The function is a polynomial almost everywhere when there is a real algebraic polynomial $p$ such that $\sigma=p$ outside a Lebesgue-null set.

The subclass $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{pt}}$ consists of those $\sigma\in\mathcal M$ that are also pointwise locally bounded: $\sup_{t\in J}|\sigma(t)|<\infty$ for every compact interval $J$. This extra condition distinguishes pointwise uniform approximation from approximation in the essential-supremum norm.

Let $d\ge1$ and let $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be an activation function. For a finite width $m\in\mathbb N_0$, output weights $a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb R$, input weights $w_1,\ldots,w_m\in\mathbb R^d$, hidden biases $b_1,\ldots,b_m\in\mathbb R$, and output bias $c\in\mathbb R$, the scalar single-hidden-layer realization is

$$N(x)=c+\sum_{j=1}^{m}a_j\sigma(w_j\cdot x+b_j),\qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

The family $\mathcal N_\sigma^{(d)}$ consists of all such functions as $m$ and the real parameters vary; $m=0$ is allowed and gives constant functions. This is the scalar-output, one-hidden-layer specialization of a layered multilayer perceptron with linear output.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$, let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be compact, and let $\sigma\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{pt}}$ not agree almost everywhere with any polynomial. Then the finite scalar single-hidden-layer networks with activation $\sigma$ are uniformly dense in $C(K,\mathbb R)$.

Let $\mu$ be a finite regular Borel measure on $\mathbb R^d$ concentrated on a compact set $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, and let $1\le p<\infty$. Form the real $L^p(\mu)$ space using the Borel $\sigma$-algebra. Then restrictions to $K$ of real-valued compactly supported continuous functions on $\mathbb R^d$ are dense in $L^p(\mu;\mathbb R)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $w\in\mathbb R^d\setminus\{0\}$, $b\in\mathbb R$, and let $E\subseteq\mathbb R$ have Lebesgue outer measure zero. Then

$$\{x\in\mathbb R^d:w\cdot x+b\in E\}$$

is Lebesgue measurable and has $d$-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero. Consequently, if two Lebesgue measurable real functions on $\mathbb R$ agree outside a null set, their compositions with the same nonconstant affine form $x\mapsto w\cdot x+b$ agree almost everywhere on $\mathbb R^d$.

Assume Countable Choice. For every integer $d\ge1$, if

$$P(x_1,\ldots,x_d)=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^d}c_\alpha x_1^{\alpha_1}\cdots x_d^{\alpha_d},$$

is a nonzero real polynomial with finitely many nonzero coefficients, then its zero set $\{x\in\mathbb R^d:P(x)=0\}$ is Lebesgue measurable and has $d$-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $q\in\mathbb N_0$, and let $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be measurable and equal almost everywhere to a polynomial of degree at most $q$ (including the zero polynomial). For every finite single-hidden-layer network with activation $\sigma$, its restriction to the segment $K=\{te_1:0\le t\le1\}\subset\mathbb R^d$ cannot approximate the target $f(te_1)=t^{q+1}$ uniformly with error less than

$$\varepsilon_q=\frac{(q+1)!}{2^{q+2}(q+1)^{q+1}}>0.$$

Consequently these networks are not uniformly dense in $C(K,\mathbb R)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $p$ be a real number with
$0<p<\infty$. Write $\mathcal M(X,\mu)$ for the measurable functions
$f:X\to\mathbb R$. For $f\in\mathcal M(X,\mu)$ define the extended-valued
$p$-functional

$$\|f\|_p:=\begin{cases}\left(\int |f|^p\,d\mu\right)^{1/p},&\displaystyle\int |f|^p\,d\mu<\infty,\\+\infty,&\displaystyle\int |f|^p\,d\mu=+\infty.\end{cases}$$

The finite power uses [[def-real-power]], while the second clause avoids
applying real powers to the extended value $+\infty$. The integral is the
nonnegative Lebesgue integral of [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]].

The class

$$\mathcal L^p(\mu):=\{f\in\mathcal M(X,\mu): \|f\|_p<\infty\}$$

is the measurable-function space used on this page before passing to
almost-everywhere equivalence classes.

For $1\le p<\infty$, the pointwise operations make $\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ a real
vector space by
[[thm-calligraphic-l-p-and-l-infinity-are-vector-spaces-for-p-at-least-one]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

- For $0<p<\infty$, define an equivalence relation on $\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ by
  $$f\sim g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f-g\in\mathcal N(\mu),$$
  and write $L^p(\mu)$ for the set of classes $[f]$.
- For $p=\infty$, define the same relation on $L^\infty(\mu)$ and again write
  $L^\infty(\mu)$ for the set of classes.

Thus an element of $L^p(\mu)$ is an almost-everywhere equivalence class of
measurable representatives.

When $1\le p\le\infty$, the displayed set quotient agrees with the usual
quotient-vector-space construction of
The quotient vector space $V/W$ and its canonical projection.

For $0<p<1$, the same class notation is used; under its stated choice hypothesis, the later item
The $L^p$ distance for $0 < p < 1$ is a complete translation-invariant metric
supplies the metric structure rather than a normed-space structure.

Let $\mu$ be a positive measure and let $
u$ be a signed measure or a complex measure on the same measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$. We say that $
u$ is **absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu$**, and write
$$
u\ll\mu,$$
if every measurable $\mu$-null set is also $
u$-null:
$$\mu(E)=0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 
u(E)=0\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$
Because every measurable subset of a $\mu$-null set is again $\mu$-null, this is equivalent to requiring $
u(F)=0$ for every measurable $F\subseteq E$ whenever $\mu(E)=0$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ (Sigma-algebras). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of Series in the nonnegative extended real line.

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. For $1\le p<\infty$, the rule
   $$\|[f]\|_p:=\|f\|_p\qquad([f]\in L^p(\mu))$$
   is well defined on the quotient classes.
2. For $p=\infty$, the rule
   $$\|[f]\|_\infty:=\|f\|_\infty\qquad([f]\in L^\infty(\mu))$$
   is well defined.
3. In either case, with the quotient vector-space operations of
   Coset equality, well-defined quotient operations, and the canonical projection with kernel $W$, the resulting pair
   $(L^p(\mu),\|\cdot\|_p)$ is a normed space in the sense of
   A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space with $\mu(X)<\infty$.

1. If $1\le p<r<\infty$ and $f\in\mathcal L^r(\mu)$, then
   $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $$\|f\|_p\le\mu(X)^{1/p-1/r}\|f\|_r.$$
2. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $$\|f\|_p\le\mu(X)^{1/p}\|f\|_\infty.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, and let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be
measurable. The **essential supremum of $|f|$ with respect to $\mu$** is

$$\|f\|_{\infty,\mu}:=\inf\{M\in[0,\infty] : |f|\le M \text{ }\mu\text{-almost everywhere}\}.$$

When the measure is fixed from context, this is written $\|f\|_\infty$. The
phrase **essentially bounded** means $\|f\|_\infty<\infty$.

The later proposition
[[prop-essential-supremum-is-attained-as-the-least-essential-bound]] proves
that when $\|f\|_\infty<\infty$, the inequality $|f|\le\|f\|_\infty$ itself
holds almost everywhere and that this bound is the least essential bound.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space,
Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
(Continuity of a map between metric spaces, at a point and globally, in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ form), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below (Lower bound, bounded below, bounded set), and it has a
maximum and a minimum (Maximum and minimum of a set): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
(Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property), Greatest lower bound (infimum)).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Every Cauchy sequence of real numbers (Limits and Cauchy sequences of reals) converges to a real
number. Together with The reals form a totally ordered field, this completes the
construction: $\mathbb{R}$ is a complete totally ordered field.
The proof uses no form of the axiom of choice.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
(The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

(Axis-parallel rectangles in $\mathbb{R}^m$ and their volume). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of Half-open boxes in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and their volume, and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ (Assuming countable choice, $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra containing every elementary set and $\lambda_n$ is a complete measure extending elementary volume).

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$. Then $E$ is
Lebesgue measurable ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]) if
and only if each of the following four conditions holds, and the four are
equivalent to one another.

1. **Open excess.** For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is an open
   $U \supseteq E$ with $\lambda_n^*(U\setminus E) < \varepsilon$.
2. **$G_\delta$ minus null.** There are a $G_\delta$ set $G$ and a set $Z$ with
   $\lambda_n^*(Z) = 0$ and $E = G\setminus Z$
   ([[def-g-delta-and-f-sigma-in-a-topological-space]]).
3. **Closed deficit.** For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a closed
   $F \subseteq E$ with $\lambda_n^*(E\setminus F) < \varepsilon$.
4. **$F_\sigma$ plus null.** There are an $F_\sigma$ set $H$ and a set $W$ with
   $\lambda_n^*(W) = 0$ and $E = H\cup W$.

Each condition is stated for sets of infinite measure as well as finite ones,
which is why the excess and the deficit are measured by the outer measure of a
difference rather than by a difference of measures.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
(The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)). Then

$$\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \;\subseteq\; \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n) :$$

every Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ (The Borel sigma-algebra of a topological space) is Lebesgue
measurable (Lebesgue measurable sets, the family $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$, and the restricted set function $\lambda_n$). In
particular every open set, every closed set and every countable intersection of
open sets is Lebesgue measurable.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). For every Lebesgue measurable
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$,

$$\lambda_n(E) \;=\; \sup\,\{\, \lambda_n(K) \;:\; K \subseteq E \text{ and } K \text{ is a compact subset of } \mathbb{R}^n \,\}$$

([[def-metric-compactness]]), the supremum being over a nonempty family since
$\varnothing$ is compact.

**The choice hypothesis is inherited, not decorative.** The proof runs through
[[thm-littlewood-characterisations-of-lebesgue-measurability]], which is itself
stated under countable choice, so the conclusion carries the same hypothesis and
says so.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: If $\sigma\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{pt}}$ is nonpolynomial almost everywhere, [F3] proves pointwise uniform density on every compact $K$. If $\sigma$ is polynomial almost everywhere, [F7] gives a specific compact segment on which density fails.

Now let $\sigma\in\mathcal M$ and put $C=\overline{D_\sigma}$, its closed null discontinuity set. Definition [F1] supplies the local essential bound and null-closure hypotheses. Define $\widetilde\sigma=\sigma$ off $C$ and $\widetilde\sigma=0$ on $C$. This is measurable and equals $\sigma$ almost everywhere. For a compact interval $J$, choose a larger compact interval $J'$ containing $J$ in its interior and an essential bound $M_{J'}$ for $\sigma$ there. At any $t\in J\setminus C$, continuity of $\sigma$ implies $|\sigma(t)|\le M_{J'}$: a strict violation would, by continuity, give an interval of positive measure inside $J'$ on which $|\sigma|>M_{J'}$. Thus $\widetilde\sigma$ is pointwise locally bounded; outside $C$ it is continuous, so the closure of its discontinuities is contained in $C$. It belongs to $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{pt}}$; if $\sigma$ is nonpolynomial almost everywhere, so is $\widetilde\sigma$. For any nonconstant affine form $T(x)=w\cdot x+b$ and any Lebesgue measurable $A\subseteq\mathbb R$, [F16] writes $A=H\cup W$ with $H$ an $F_\sigma$ set and $W$ outer null. Then $T^{-1}(H)$ is Borel, hence Lebesgue measurable by [F17], and $T^{-1}(W)$ is measurable and null by [F5]. Thus $\sigma\circ T$ is Lebesgue measurable, as is every finite network; constant affine forms give constant measurable units. This makes the essential-supremum seminorm in the Statement well-defined for raw networks.

For the converse, suppose $\sigma=p_0$ almost everywhere for a polynomial $p_0$ of degree $q$. By [F5] and [F8], every nonconstant unit equals $p_0(w_j\cdot x+b_j)$ for $\mu$-almost every $x$; constant-input units can be absorbed into the output bias. Hence every network represents, in $L^p(\mu)$, a polynomial of total degree at most $q$.

For any finite $\widetilde\sigma$-network, a unit with $w_j\ne0$ differs from the corresponding $\sigma$-unit only on the null pullback $\{x:w_j\cdot x+b_j\in C\}$, null by [F5]. Replace the output bias by $c+\sum_{w_j=0}a_j(\widetilde\sigma(b_j)-\sigma(b_j))$ to absorb the constant-input units. The resulting $\sigma$-network equals the $\widetilde\sigma$-network almost everywhere in $\mathbb R^d$, and hence defines the same Borel $L^p(\mu)$ class under the representative convention when $\mu\ll\lambda_d$. For nonpolynomial-almost-everywhere $\sigma$, applying [F3] to $\widetilde\sigma$ and transferring these approximants proves essential-supremum density for $\mathcal M$ on every compact $K$.

Assume $\mu(K)>0$ and let $P_q$ be the vector space of real polynomials in $d$ variables of total degree at most $q$. In a monomial basis its coefficient space is $\mathbb R^s$ for some finite $s\ge1$, with its Euclidean norm. Every monomial is bounded on compact $K$, so for coefficient vectors $a,b$ one has $\sup_K|P_a-P_b|\le\sum_{|\alpha|\le q}|a_\alpha-b_\alpha|\sup_K|x^\alpha|$, which tends to zero as $a-b\to0$. By [F12], $\|P_a-P_b\|_{L^p(\mu)}\le\mu(K)^{1/p}\sup_K|P_a-P_b|$; the reverse triangle inequality from [F11] therefore makes $P\mapsto\|P\|_{L^p(\mu)}$ continuous in the coefficients. For a nonzero coefficient vector, $P$ is a nonzero polynomial; by [F6] its zero set is Lebesgue null, hence $\mu$-null by [F8]. If its $L^p$ norm were zero, [F11] would make its class zero, so $P=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere. This would give $\mu(K\setminus\{P=0\})=0$, whereas [F8] and [F10] give $\mu(K\setminus\{P=0\})=\mu(K)>0$, a contradiction. Thus the norm is positive on the coefficient unit sphere. That sphere is nonempty and compact by [F9], and [F13] gives a minimum $a>0$; homogeneity yields $\|P\|_{L^p(\mu)}\ge a|\operatorname{coeff}(P)|$. Any $L^p$-Cauchy sequence in $P_q$ therefore has Cauchy coefficient vectors. By [F14], their finitely many coordinates converge to those of a polynomial $P\in P_q$; the coefficient estimate above and [F12] imply convergence to $P$ in $L^p$. If a class lies in the closure of $P_q$, Countable Choice [A1] supplies a sequence from $P_q$ converging to it; the preceding argument and uniqueness of norm limits [F11] put that class in $P_q$. Hence $P_q$ is closed in $L^p(\mu)$.

To justify the Borel convention, $C$ is closed, $\widetilde\sigma=0$ on $C$, and $\widetilde\sigma$ is continuous on the open complement of $C$, so $\widetilde\sigma$ is Borel measurable.
